stories.sourceMaterial: Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover ’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos , the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute. NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars. ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October , seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos. This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth. “I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” says Yasuhiro Kawakatsu , project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.” Why Phobos Is Such a Strange Moon Phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos , named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites. The enormous Stickney crater, roughly 9 kilometers across, dominates this view of Phobos taken by NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800 th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth. More than 10 years in the making, MMX launched on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA. Engineers assembled MMX’s modules at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center before the spacecraft’s October 2026 launch. JAXA MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home. If all goes according to plan, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth. The MMX’s modular design includes the propulsion module [left] and the exploration and return modules [right]. Kyodo News/Getty Images “It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” says Patrick Michel , director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix. How MMX Will Orbit Phobos An H3 rocket carried MMX into space on 20 October 2026, beginning the mission’s five-year journey to Phobos and back. The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images Once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The museum opened its doors as part of the 1976 Bicentennial festivities and is the nation’s oldest public collection of bonsai and related arts. “As we mark the National Bonsai & Penjing Museum's 50th anniversary, we celebrate a unique chapter in the U.S. National Arboretum's history and a lasting symbol of international goodwill,” said USDA Under Secretary Dr. Scott Hutchins. “Throughout the past five decades, the museum continues to connect people through art, horticulture, and cultural exchange, and I celebrate this golden anniversary as we honor both the extraordinary trees in our care and the friendship that brought them here." The National Bonsai & Penjing Museum began with the “original gift” of 53 bonsai and 6 viewing stones, 200th birthday presents from the people of Japan to the people of the United States. The gift was shepherded by then-USNA director Dr. John Creech. Why 53 trees? Bonsai artists from across Japan had collaborated to donate 50 trees, in honor of the 50 American states. The Imperial family gave three more trees, including one from the emperor’s personal collection—the first time such a tree had ever been allowed to leave Japan. Bonsai trees at the National Bonsai & Penjing Museum “For half a century, the National Bonsai & Penjing Museum has brought together art, horticulture, research, and international collaboration,” said Joon Park, Administrator of USDA’s Agricultural Research Service. “This extraordinary collection preserves decades of history, craftsmanship, and cultural exchange while serving as a living resource for education and research. As we celebrate its first 50 years, we also recognize the opportunities ahead to advance our understanding of plant health, helping to inspire new discoveries.” Since the original gift, the museum has progressed into a comprehensive collection illustrating the artform’s adoption, evolution, and influence across geographies and throughout time. The museum’s current collection contains 200+ trees from 6 countries, including the work of North American artists as well as North American native species. It is one of the main attractions for visitors to the National Arboretum, with trees displayed in three open-air pavilions and an enclosed building to showcase viewing stones (over 270 stones collected in Asia, Europe, Africa, and North America) and temporary exhibits. In honor of the bonsai collection’s anniversary, the USNA presents: Branching Out: 50 Years of Bonsai at the National Arboretum , with the following celebratory events: November 6, 2026 : Private ceremony to formally accept 10 bonsai and 3 viewing stones (suiseki) into the Museum’s collections, with distinguished speakers detailing the history, legacy, and impact of the Museum’s 50 years. A small reception in the Museum will follow. November 7, 2026 : A public day of celebration from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The day begins with a ribbon cutting at the Museum’s gates, ushering in the next half-century of bonsai education, training, and research. The day will feature the public debut of the newly acquired bonsai and suiseki and the opening of a history exhibit exploring the Museum’s history. Activities include docent-led museum tours, bonsai maintenance demonstrations by the 2026 National Bonsai Apprentice, screenings of the documentary Bicentennial Bonsai: Emissaries of Peace, and children’s activities. November 7, 2026 : At 6 p.m., the USNA is hosting its first-ever science café ( tickets required ). Guests will enjoy beverages and a series of engaging, short presentations by scientists revealing the scientific mysteries of bonsai growth and maintenance. Guests can also enjoy an evening stroll in the Museum, a rare opportunity. The USNA has a dual scientific and public horticulture mission. It is administered by the USDA’s Agricultural Research Service. In the next 50 years, the USNA aims to advance the scientific understanding of bonsai horticulture—the important yet un-studied practical complement to the artistic and cultural significance of bonsai and penjing collections. By recognizing and acting on the scientific opportunities within the Museum, the USNA deepens the educational opportunities and provides a significant benefit to the bonsai community. Visit the USNA website ( www.usna.usda.gov ) or follow the Friends of the National Arboretum ( www.fona.org ) for additional details.
